blocks.content: By eight-thirty, Ethan was back at The Copper Mug with his sketchbook under one arm.
Mr. Alvarez had already unlocked the front door and placed Ethan's cup on the counter before Ethan ordered.

blocks.speaker: Mr. Alvarez
blocks.content: You are late.
Ethan glanced at the clock.

blocks.speaker: Ethan
blocks.content: You opened three minutes ago.

blocks.speaker: Mr. Alvarez
blocks.content: Late.

blocks.speaker: Ethan
blocks.content: I ran farther.

blocks.speaker: Mr. Alvarez
blocks.content: Excuses are free. Coffee is not.
Ethan smiled despite himself.

blocks.speaker: Ethan
blocks.content: Morning to you too.

blocks.speaker: Mr. Alvarez
blocks.content: Two sugars. Because bitterness should only exist in art.

blocks.speaker: Ethan
blocks.content: That's actually a good line.

blocks.speaker: Mr. Alvarez
blocks.content: You may paint it on my wall for half price.

blocks.speaker: Ethan
blocks.content: I'll consider being exploited.

blocks.speaker: Mr. Alvarez
blocks.content: That is the spirit of capitalism.
Ethan paid and took the corner table near the window. His table. Not officially. Unofficially enough that the other regulars left it alone.
He opened his sketchbook to a blank page and tapped his pencil once against the paper.
Blank pages never scared him. People did.
He stared out the window. Town was fully awake now. Delivery trucks. A woman carrying flowers. Two kids arguing outside the bakery over who got the bigger pastry.
He began sketching the street without thinking too hard. That was usually when his best work happened.
A line for the curb. The bookstore sign. The bakery awning. People as motion first, detail second.
Then red hair.
His pencil paused.

Across the street, the girl from the bus walked beside another girl with dark curly hair — laughing, shoulders nearly bumping, both carrying drinks. The red-haired girl had a stuffed purple dinosaur tucked under one arm like a trophy.
She actually won something from that machine.
She turned backward as she walked, talking to her friend, hands cutting shapes in the air. The dinosaur nearly slipped. She caught it and laughed again.
People looked at her. Not in a strange way. The way people looked at something bright passing through a room.
Ethan looked down at his page.
Without meaning to, he had drawn her outline into the street scene. Not her face. Just movement. The tilt of her shoulders. The wild fall of her hair. The dinosaur under her arm.
Great. Sketching random strangers. Completely normal behavior.
He flipped the page quickly — not before noticing Mr. Alvarez watching him from behind the counter.
Ethan cleared his throat and became very interested in his coffee.
Mr. Alvarez lifted one eyebrow. Ethan ignored him. Tried to.
The bell above the door jingled. For one panicked second, Ethan thought she had come inside.
She hadn't. Just an elderly man in a brown coat.
Ethan exhaled slowly.
Relax. You saw a pretty girl. Civilization will recover.
He glanced out the window anyway.
She was gone. The street looked ordinary again.
